2.21. SERVICE LEVEL BENCHMARKING
The guidelines and toolkit issued by MoHUA for the preparation of CMP suggests the
comparative analysis of Urban Transport environment with benchmark values
suggested in the toolkit as the Level of Service (LOS). The urban transport scenario in
Jaipur has been evaluated and compared with benchmarks to diagnose the existing
transport condition and to identify urgent areas for improvement in the city.
To facilitate comparison between cities and changes in performance over time, it is
important that the performance levels are monitored against set benchmarks. It is in
this context that the toolkit defines SLBs for various parameters of urban transport.
SLBs have been identified for the following parameters:
i. Public transport facilities
ii. Pedestrian infrastructure facilities
iii. Non-Motorized Transport (NMT) facilities
iv. Level of usage of Intelligent Transport System (ITS) facilities
v. Travel speed (Motorized and Mass Transit) along major corridors
vi. Availability of parking spaces
vii. Road safety
viii. Pollution levels
ix. Integrated land use transport system
x. Financial sustainability of public transport
These parameters highlight the performance of urban transport in the city. Typically,
four LOS viz. 1, 2, 3, and 4 have been specified, with 1 being the highest LOS and 4
being lowest to measure each identified performance benchmark. Therefore, the goal
is to attain service level 1.

3. TRANSPORT DEMAND ASSESSMENT
3.1. DEVELOPMENT OF BUSINESS AS USUAL SCENARIOS
3.1.1. COVERAGE
The travel demand assessment in urban environment is a complex exercise
involving a large number of parameters and warrants the development of a travel
model at the city level. The travel demand modelling process consists of the
development of formulae (or models), enabling forecast of travel demand, and
development of alternative strategies for handling this demand. It is not just one
model, but a series of interlinked and interrelated models of varying levels of
complexity, dealing with different facets of travel demand. Through these models,
the transportation study process as a whole is checked and calibrated before it is
used for future travel predictions.
While a number of commercially acceptable softwares are available for the purpose
of modelling travel demand, due heed was paid to the observed traffic
heterogeneity in the study area. After analysing specific model requirements and
software compatibility, PTV VISUM software is recommended for modelling
exercise for the study.
Detailed traffic and travel surveys have been carried out as part of the assignment
to establish the existing and future travel demand. The operational travel demand
model is also a prerequisite so that consultants are able to validate actual travel
patterns (as observed) within an acceptable error range (+-15%). The standard 4
stage Urban Transport Planning System model has been adopted that inter alia
consists of:
• Stage 1 - Trip Generation and Attraction Sub Model
• Stage 2 - Trip Distribution Sub Model
• Stage 3 - Modal Split Sub Model
• Stage 4 - Assignment Sub Model
A commuter decides on his/ her selection of travel modes, considering a number of
parameters, including accessibility of travel mode from the house, total travel time,
total cost of travel, convenience/ comfort of travel and cost/ convenience for
reaching the destination at the other end of the main journey. The commuter
evaluates the merits and demerits of all possible alternative modes and their
combinations before deciding on the final selection of travel mode(s).
Updated base maps for identified locations, areas, junctions and intersections
collected from the respective agencies as a part of secondary data collection

transport network consisting of primary and secondary road network was coded in
PTV VISUM. The link attributes such as speed, carriageway, ROW, length etc. are
derived from Inventory, Speed and Delay survey data.
Major inputs to an urban travel demand model may be summarized as below:
• Delineation of study area into smaller traffic zones, road and public transport
network along with their attributes
• Population and employment (existing and proposed at traffic zone level)
• Various transport systems along with their capacity, headways and speed etc.
• Intermodal integration facilities available and time required for passengers to
interchange from one mode to another including walk time.

Four sub models viz. Trip Generation, Trip Distribution, Modal Split and Assignment

The model development is largely based on the data from Household Interview
Survey (HIS) and other primary travel surveys after expansion of the survey samples

calculated at traffic zone level.
The next step was to build the base year matrices necessary to obtain costs for the
model development (distribution and modal choice). The base year HIS person
matrices converted to vehicles using occupancy factors, trip matrices, external
zones matrices from roadside interview at Outer Cordon locations and special
generators (bus, airport railway station and tourists) matrices to get total traffic
across the Study Area.
a) Trip Generation Model
The two components of trip generation modelling are:
Trip Production: This is defined as the home end of a home-based trip or as the
origin of a non-home-based trip. It thus gives the total trips produced by a
zone.
Trip Attraction: This is defined as the non-home end of a home-based trip or as
the destination of a non-home-based trip. It thus, gives the total trips attracted
to a zone.
The factors that may affect trip generation include land use factors such as

population, employment, intensity of residential activity and employment
opportunities etc. Other household factors including household income etc. also
affects the trips generated.
Trip Purpose: The purpose of trip can be broadly categorized in home based trips &
non-home based trips. Home based trips are those in which one of either trip ends
is at home while non-home based are those in which neither end is at home.
Different transportation studies have adapted different classification systems for
trip purpose depending upon the planning issues involved and the size of city. The
trip generation model has been developed for home based trips in aggregation.
(i) Trip Production Sub Model

attraction equations. A zonal regression model is used in which each traffic zone is
treated as one observation. The aggregated analysis is applied for developing the

households exhibit a certain amount of similarity in travel characteristics. This
assumption allows the data in a zone to be grouped and the mean value of the
independent variable used in further calculations. The general form of the work trip

Mode choice models have been developed for all modes of transport including
public transport and intermediate paratransit modes. For our study, mode choice
has been computed based on revealed preference of individuals surveyed in the
household survey. A multi-nominal logit or Nested logit models has been run to

The total trips are split into two major group of ‘Private’ and ‘Public’ mode of travel.
Private modes are further divided into Car, 2W and auto. PT trips consist of Buses
and Shared Autorickshaws. It should be noted that the PT matrix produced by the

3.2. DEVELOPMENT OF SUSTAINABLE URBAN TRANSPORT SCENARIOS
3.2.1. FRAMEWORK FOR SCENARIOS
Business As Usual (BAU) scenario with decreasing share of public transport, Non-
Motorized Transport (NMT) and walk, will not lead the city towards national goals
of sustainable transport and climate change. In order to achieve these goals,
Landuse, Public Transport, NMT and Technological Transitions have been
considered as strategies for developing various Sustainable Urban Transport (SUT)
scenarios. It is expected that adoption of the SUT scenario will fulfill the objective of
enhancing economic and social development while mitigating CO emissions within
2
the city. This will enable the city to handle the mobility challenges while considering
climate change and the local environment. The SUT scenarios are based on the
following principles:
• Changes in urban structure
• Enhanced use of non-motorized and public transport infrastructures
• Deep emission cuts using low carbon energy sources
• Use of highly efficient technologies in vehicles
CMP will identify investment priorities to help achieve the sustainable transport
goals. Though the sustainable scenarios will assume an increase in motorized
transport to some extent, emphasis has been placed on improving technology in
terms of efficiency and emissions. Following four SUT Scenarios have been
formulated:
• Urban Structure Scenario: Intensive development along high demand PT
corridors.
• Public Transport Scenario: In addition to Scenario 1, augmentation of PT
system.

a. URBAN STRUCTURE SCENARIO
i. Landuse Transition
Urban sprawl and uncontrolled growth of cities result into increase in trip lengths
which is not desirable. Accordingly, compact development of the city is envisaged
with high density and multi-nuclei development to increase share of walk and NMT
and improve access to public transport. To achieve higher density and compact
development, changes in planning and regulatory measures such as zoning
regulations and floor area ratio (FAR) are required.
The BAU scenario considers land use pattern as proposed by the Master Plan -
2025, concentrating the commercial activity in different areas of city. Planning new
February 2026 Page 3-22
Comprehensive Mobility Plan for Jaipur City
Draft CMP Chapter 3: Transport Demand Assessment
commercial activities to outgrowths of the city would result in better distribution of
population and employment, decongesting the core areas as people in the
outgrowths would not need to travel to the core city for their work, shopping and
other activities. However, this would not discourage the use of motorized modes of
transport and will increase the carbon footprint of the city.
As such, in the Urban Structure Scenario, an alternative pattern of city growth is
envisaged where the commercial activity is spread across the entire city, primarily
along the major travel demand corridors. This scenario will promote a better urban
structure for the city and will also ensure the success of an organized public
transport in the city.
ii. Projections and Distribution of Population in Urban Structure Scenario
The urban structure strategy envisages higher population along the major travel
corridors. Accordingly, some of the high demand corridors identified under the BAU
scenario are planned to be developed intensively by increase in FSI/FAR. This
presents us with three categories of Traffic Analysis Zones (TAZ) namely:
• Class 1: Zones along major travel corridors
• Class 2: Core Area Zones
• Class 3: Non-Core Area Zones
While the overall population for the city is same as that of BAU scenario, the
distribution of population by traffic zones changes in the Urban Structure scenario
in accordance with the above classification of TAZs. The overall population growth
in Class 1 is assumed to be more than 100% from the year 2024 to year 2055, the
population in Class 2 and 3 TAZ is assumed to be increased by 40 - 45%. The final
population for the three classifications of zones is about 45.20 Lakh, 15.19 Lakh and
40.92 Lakh for Class 1, 2 and 3 respectively in the year 2055 totaling to 101.31 Lakh.
It is expected that the increase in FSI/FAR will not only concentrate the population
along travel corridors but will also marginally induce population in the city, not
reflected in the projections for BAU scenario. An additional population of about 2%
of the base year population (1.12 Lakh) is assumed to be induced as indirect effect
of the land use transitions under this scenario.
Based on the above assumptions, the city's population projected for the year 2055
is 102.43 lakh.

B. PUBLIC TRANSPORT SCENARIO
With urban expansion and increasing economic prosperity, there is an increase in
vehicle ownership and in the absence of safe and reliable public transport people
are forced to use private vehicles for their travel needs. Public transport can serve
to mitigate the economic and environmental burden that increased vehicle
ownership has imposed on the city or population. This improvement goes beyond
infrastructure development to include better accessibility, integration with land
use, and non-motorized transport (NMT) infrastructure.
In this scenario, public transport infrastructure is envisioned to be upgraded
through the introduction of Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS) along major travel
corridors, offering enhanced comfort and safety compared to existing modes. Low-
capacity transport modes will be deployed on arterial and minor roads with limited
right-of-way. Improved scheduling, increased network coverage, and enhanced
safety and comfort for users are central to this scenario.
Existing shared autos will be the competing modes which may impact the ridership
of MRTS. Therefore, the operation of shared autos is planned to operate as a feeder
to MRTS routes. In addition to the improved service, rail-based mass rapid transit
system on selected high demand corridors is considered in this scenario. All these
improvements are factored into the transport demand model for the horizon year
of 2054.
The Urban Structure scenario’s growth patterns, modulated to increase public
transport accessibility, serve as the baseline for this iterative analysis. The goal is to
encourage a modal shift from private vehicles to public transport. This scenario
expects a significant shift from two-wheeler use to public transport, with minimal
changes in the modal share of cycling and walking compared to the Urban Structure
scenario.

c. NON- MOTORIZED TRANSPORT SCENARIO
Non-Motorized Transport (NMT) modes are the cleanest modes and interventions
for the infrastructure improvement of NMT modes are necessary for sustainable
urban transport in the city. As such, this scenario is assumed to increase the modal
share of walk and NMT in the city. This results in a high level of pedestrian vehicular
conflict and high fatalities. Safe walking and cycling infrastructure is envisaged
under this scenario for better safety and to promote walk and NMT as a preferred
mode in the city in addition to the interventions considered under Urban Structure
and Public Transport scenarios.
The assumed infrastructure under the NMT scenario will include continuous
footpaths and cycle paths, good crossing facilities, parking for cyclists, signal
prioritization, strong parking policies and strict enforcement to remove the
hindrances on NMT infrastructures. The modal share derived from travel demand
model is presented in TABLE 3.19.

d. TECHNOLOGY TRANSITION
The Technology Transition scenario is envisaged in progression to the NMT
scenario. Though under the NMT scenario, there is an increment in the share of
NMT and walk trips, substantial share of trips will continue to be catered by
motorized modes including public transport modes as bus and shared autos. As
such, it is imperative to reduce consumption of conventional sources of energy for
motorized modes. Fuel mix shares used as inputs to estimation of emissions of CO
2
and other pollutants for year 2055 based on Niti Aayog RMI Study May 2017 are
summarized in TABLE 3.20 and Fuel Consumption for various scenarios is given in

In the modeling framework, the fuel mix for public transport (PT) has been adjusted
in the Public Transport and Non-Motorised Transport (NMT) scenarios to reflect the
increased emphasis on sustainable and shared mobility options, as compared to the
Urban Structure scenario. These scenarios prioritize modal shift towards public
transport, thereby necessitating a corresponding change in the fuel composition to
support expanded and cleaner PT operations.
Furthermore, under the Technology Scenario, it is assumed that advancements in
vehicle and fuel technologies by the year 2055 will lead to significant improvements
in fuel efficiency across all modes. Hence, an increase in fuel efficiency has been
incorporated into the scenario assumptions, reflecting the expected benefits of
evolving transport technologies and cleaner propulsion systems.

4.1. INTEGRATED LAND USE AND URBAN MOBILITY PLAN
Urban transport is a derived demand that is intrinsically shaped by land use patterns,
while the presence and quality of transport infrastructure simultaneously influence
urban development. The integration of land use and transportation systems is
fundamental to achieving sustainable urban growth. As outlined in the National Urban
Transport Policy (NUTP), 2014, it is essential that transport and land use planning be
undertaken concurrently, ensuring inclusivity while reducing the need for travel.
An integrated master plan must embed the principles of sustainable urban transport
from the outset. This entails guiding a city’s future expansion around a strategically
designed transport network, rather than reacting to unplanned urban sprawl. In
alignment with this approach, the present study proposes the formulation of an
Integrated Land Use and Urban Mobility Plan to support holistic and future-ready urban
development.
4.1.1. Recommended Urban Structure
The Jaipur Master Plan – 2025 outlines a land use strategy that distributes commercial
activities across various zones, including the city’s core. However, this decentralized
approach is likely to promote increased reliance on motorized transportation, resulting
in higher emissions and a greater carbon footprint. To address these concerns, the
present study recommends a shift towards intensive urban development along key
travel demand corridors. This strategy would enable the implementation of high-
capacity public transport systems, ensuring efficient passenger movement while
supporting environmentally sustainable growth.
a) Recommended FAR
The Government of Rajasthan has notified the Transit Oriented Development (TOD)
Policy 2025 to promote compact, mixed-use, and transit-supportive urban development
along major public transport corridors.
The policy prescribes mixed-use distribution and development intensity through
defined Built-up Area Ratio (BAR) in place of FAR norms based on existing land use and
scheme category. A balanced mix of residential, commercial, and public/semi-public
uses is ensured, while retaining minimum proportions of the original land use. The
required mix may be achieved either horizontally across plots or vertically within
buildings, subject to compatibility and safety considerations. BAR for a TOD scheme is

Category-1 and Category-2 schemes, the base BAR is as per prevailing Building Bye-laws,
with an enhanced TOD BAR of up to 3.0, subject to a minimum ROW of 12 m. Building
height is regulated in relation to ROW and front setback, capped at 1.75 times the ROW
plus front setback, while maximum ground coverage is limited to 50% for schemes up
to 1 ha and 45% for schemes above 1 ha. Additional purchasable BAR beyond 3.0 is
permitted on payment of a betterment levy, varying by land use and BAR slab, enabling
value capture from intensified development.

a) Short Term (0-5 Years) - Traffic Engineering & Management Measures
Traffic engineering and management interventions have been finalized based on the
identified mobility challenges and are included in this report. The proposed schemes
include the following key measures:
▪ Junction Improvements: Geometric enhancements to facilitate efficient turning
movements, including the provision of channelisers and traffic islands.
▪ Corridor Upgrades: Traffic circulation improvements along major corridors,
including strengthening and redesigning footpaths for pedestrian safety and
convenience.

infrastructure for pedestrians and cyclists to promote safe, sustainable, and
inclusive mobility.

4.2. PUBLIC TRANSPORT IMPROVEMENT PLAN
The public transportation system is planned on a combination of high-capacity trunk
and medium-capacity corridors. The balance network is proposed for low-capacity
feeder systems operations.
The high-capacity trunk corridors are primarily envisioned to be served by Mass Rapid
Transit System, which is suitable for corridors with high passenger demand, adequate
Right of Way (ROW), and dense land-use patterns. The selection of these trunk corridors
depend mainly on the expected public transport demand and the availability of ROW.
Other considerations are the land-use along the corridor, the location of building lines,
and the potential for increasing the ROW.
Using the same principle, mass rapid transit system has been proposed on high-capacity
trunk corridors while Bus/Intermediate Public Transport (IPT) system has been
proposed on other medium to low capacity corridors. The description of same has been
given in subsequent sections.
4.2.1. Proposed Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS) Corridors
Considering the public transport demand for the horizon period of 30 years, the master
plan for Mass Rapid Transit System has been proposed for the next 30 years. The Phase
1 MRTS corridor is already operational. The MRTS corridors have been proposed to be

To enable the shift from existing intermediate public transport modes (Shared

feeder mode to nodes on the bus corridors providing last-mile connectivity.
b) City E-Bus System
A shift towards clean energy for public transport brings multi-dimensional benefits. The
induction of E-buses will add to the emission reduction commitments at the local level.
However, the use of motorized modes of transport will increase the carbon footprint of
the city. Electric buses, when compared to the conventional bus, have fewer moving
parts. This results in lower and more predictable operating costs. The dependence on
fossil fuels poses uncertainties due to price fluctuations, while the cost of electricity is
stable for e-buses.
The buses have been proposed with following specifications:
• Modern low floor buses, each with two wide doors allowing passengers to board
and alight quickly and easily and 8 passengers can alight at a time.
• Considering the geometry of the road, severe congestion, haphazard parking
short wheelbase buses will be suitable to run in the city. The buses should have
an optimum capacity for sitting and standing passengers based on the passenger
demand. It will save time and improve per kilometre performance.
• The E-buses which have been allotted to city under FAME India scheme Phase-II
are of 9 m in length.

recommendations have been proposed to improve their operations:
• Appropriate parking/stands at all locations, such as:
o Commercial areas like shopping malls and retail areas
o Public spaces like parks and tourist locations
o Residential colonies: each colony to have an authorized auto-rickshaw
stand.
• Dedicated parking lot with facilities like drinking water, toilet and maintenance
facility
• Stopping and boarding facilities in sync with bus-stops so that the shared auto
services are integrated with city buses and act as a feeder mode to them.
• Shared autos to be used as both a primary public transport system in the
outgrowth areas where the demand is not justified as bus system, and as a
feeder service to city buses in other areas based on corridor demand.
• Shared auto‐ rickshaws should be issued route permits/ licenses across mobility
corridors.
• Existing diesel autos are the major contributor of pollution in the city. It is
therefore proposed to roll out the existing diesel autos in phases. Shared autos
may be replaced with e-autos in phases. This will promote environmental
sustainability by achieving low carbon emissions.

4.3.1. Mobility Corridors
Jaipur city exhibits a radial and grid-iron pattern of road network, with its major radial
roads functioning as the arterial corridors of the city. These arterials carry a significant
share of intra-city traffic and act as the primary mobility spines connecting different

Comprehensive Mobility Plan for Jaipur City

parts of Jaipur. Historically, the radial roads originated from the walled city area
extending outward and integrating with the newer grid-based developments. Over
time, these arterial roads have become key corridors linking the core city to peripheral
growth centers. Jaipur is also traversed by two major National Highways—NH 48 (Delhi–
Ajmer–Mumbai Corridor) and NH 52 (Jaipur–Kota–Bhopal Corridor)—which serve both
regional and urban functions, facilitating through traffic, freight movement, and city-
level connectivity. Following mobility corridors have been identified:
a. Outer Ring Road
The Southern Alignment of the Outer Ring Road (47 km) is completed and operational.
This section functions as a major bypass for through traffic while simultaneously
promoting planned urban expansion along the southern periphery of Jaipur.
The Northern Alignment of the Outer Ring Road (ORR) as shown in FIGURE 4.9. The
proposed Northern Outer Ring Road (ORR) is planned to traverse through the peripheral
areas of Bagru, Pachar, Jaitpura, Achrol, and Bhanpur Kalan forming a strategic
circumferential corridor around the northern edge of the urban area and connecting the
satellite towns. The total length of the proposed northern alignment is approximately
99 km.
The main transport corridor of the Ring Road is planned as a 90 m wide strip, for
development of a 6-lane access-controlled carriageway (3 lanes on each side, with
median and service facilities). Service roads / slip roads are proposed along either side
within the remaining width to segregate through traffic from local access. The
Development Corridor / PAP Corridor (135 m on either side) will accommodate
supporting infrastructure such as utility corridors, feeder roads, drainage, landscaping,
and resettlement
The Northern Ring Road alignment is strategically designed to divert heavy vehicular
traffic away from Jaipur city, enhance high-speed connectivity between highways, and
unlock growth potential in underdeveloped peripheral areas. The alignment will also
improve access to emerging urban nodes, industrial clusters, and satellite towns. The
final detailing of the northern portion, including the tunnel and junction designs, may
be undertaken at the implementation stage to ensure optimum efficiency, safety, and
environmental sustainability.

b. Grade Separated Facilities
To address rising traffic congestion at critical junctions and along high-volume corridors,
grade-separated facilities such as flyovers, underpasses, and elevated corridors are
proposed at key locations across Jaipur. These grade-separated facilities are planned
along major arterial and sub-arterial roads where surface capacity is inadequate, and
right-of-way expansion is constrained. The elevated corridors will facilitate the
uninterrupted movement of through traffic, particularly along radial routes connecting
to the city core, while flyovers/underpasses at junctions will ease conflict points and
reduce travel delays. Together, these interventions aim to improve average travel
speeds, enhance safety, and strengthen connectivity between the city’s radial network,
ring road system, and national highways.
To relieve traffic congestion, flyovers/ underpasses are being planned by NHAI and JDA
in the city. The following proposals for grade-separated facilities have been proposed in
integration with NHAI and JDA proposals for the city:
• A total of 14 grade-separated road infrastructure projects comprising flyovers,
elevated roads, and underpasses have been identified to address major
congestion points and improve corridor-level traffic movement within the city.
• The proposals include flyovers at key junctions such as Todi Mod (0.6 km), Nindar
Mod (0.7 km), Vijay Dwar (0.8 km), Bilwa (1.8 km), Kanouta Junction (1.0 km),
and New Sanganer Road–Bhagat Singh Chouraha (0.8 km) to facilitate
uninterrupted through movement.
• Elevated road corridors have been proposed along high traffic stretches,
including Aranya Bhawan to Jagatpura ROB (4.4 km) and Chauradiya Petrol Pump
to Sanganer Circle (1.2 km) to enhance corridor capacity.
• Underpasses are proposed at critical conflict locations such as Gopalpura Puliya
(0.7 km) and Mansarovar Road to Delhi Road at 200 ft Bypass (0.6 km) to
segregate traffic streams and reduce delays.
• At the 14 No. Road Junction (NH-48 and NH-52), a grade-separated solution
(flyover/underpass) of approximately 0.8 km has been proposed to improve

• Additional connectivity improvements include link flyovers and directional
ramps, such as the flyover connecting DCM Road to the existing Ajmer Road

4.4. NON-MOTORISED TRANSPORT IMPROVEMENT PLAN
NMT and pedestrian infrastructure are fundamental components of sustainable
transport for Jaipur. The development of NMT facilities is proposed as an integral part
of the city’s overall road development and mobility improvement program. To promote
NMT usage, priority must be accorded to pedestrian and Non-Motorized Vehicle (NMV)
safety, which can be achieved through effective segregation from motorized traffic.
In Jaipur, footpaths are not present on all the major arterial roads where high pedestrian
footfall is observed, and wherever available, they are often underutilized. The
discontinuity of footpaths at frequent intervals—caused by encroachments, design
deficiencies, utility obstructions, and deterioration—makes them inconvenient and
unsafe for regular use. Similarly, NMV lanes/ cycle tracks are completely absent in the
network.
To improve the NMT scenario in Jaipur, it is crucial not only to increase the coverage
and connectivity of pedestrian and NMV facilities, but also to ensure their continuity,
accessibility, and regular upkeep. This will enhance safety, promote walking and cycling,
and contribute to a more inclusive and sustainable mobility system in the city.
The proposals under Non-Motorized Transport (NMT) Improvement Plan are:
• Development of Footpaths
• Providing Foot over Bridges (FOBs)
• Development of cycle lanes
• Public bike sharing scheme
• At grade Pedestrian Crossing Facilities
4.4.1. Proposed Footpath Network
Pedestrian excursions are often brief and may be found throughout a city. As a result,
pedestrian walkways should ideally be provided on all main arterial roads and streets.
However, pedestrians should be given extra care around crossings (dangerous
intersections), and significant activity hubs (like schools, colleges, etc.). The design of
the city's footpaths should be consistent. The city requires pathways with a minimum
width of 1.8 m. For higher footfall areas (commercial/transport hubs) the minimum
width of footpath shall be 4.0 m.
Jaipur being city having higher pedestrian footfall, shall consider the following for
footpath:
• Minimum width of footpath in Residential Streets / Local Roads must be 1.8 m.
• Minimum width of footpath in Collector Roads / Secondary Arterials must be
2.5m.

4.4.4. Public E-BIKE Sharing (PBS)
Public Bike Sharing (PBS) is a high-quality bicycle based public transport system in which
bicycles, stored in a closely spaced network of stations, are made available for short-
term shared use. Bicycle sharing programs involve installing multiple bicycle stations at
several different key locations. A user checks-out the bicycle from one location, rides to
his or her destination, and drops the bicycle to another location. The operators
coordinate the redistribution of bicycles and ensure availability of cycles at locations
with the highest demand at any given time.”
Public Bicycle Sharing (PBS) is slowly emerging as one of the most sustainable, popular
and attractive public transport modes throughout the world. This mode offers the
conveniences of both public and personal modes. It enables public access to personal
bicycles, offering maximum flexibility with minimum liability.
a. Objectives For E-Bike Sharing Scheme
• To provide affordable last-mile connectivity options for public transit systems.
• To connect all the trip’s origins and destinations to public transit systems via e-
bike sharing.
The benefits of E-Bike sharing are listed below:
• It encourages equitable distribution of infrastructure to all the citizens and users
of the city.
• It mobilizes not only the movement but also the improved health conditions of
the end users in terms of mental and physical well-being of the community.
• It also helps in creating the balance and harmony of a healthy environment for
the city by mitigating the climate change response.
• It boosts end user’s safety throughout the trip by making it more viable against a
motorized vehicle to avoid collisions and damage.
• It requires cheaper and affordable interventions in terms of infrastructure
alignment. Also, it is easy to operate, maintain and monitor for longer
generations. Thus, providing economic value.
• Overall, it benefits citizens and makes the journey more enjoyable. Thus,
benefiting the city in terms of providing ideal quality of life.
b. Components of E-Bike Sharing Scheme

4.6.4. Proposed Freight Terminals
The presence of various RIICO industries and Kanakpura Dry Port results in generation
of substantial amount of freight traffic. Further, Jaipur Region falls in between the busy
corridor connecting Delhi and Mumbai. The timely and smooth movement of such
freight is crucial to the well-being of the people and the viability of the economic
activities they undertake. Considerable goods movement is observed along major
highways like NH-48, NH-52, NH-21, NH-248, SH-12, SH-2C, and SH-55. However, the
entry of heavy vehicles to the core city has been restricted during the daytime and is
allowed only during late night hours (11 pm to 4 am).
Transport Nagar located on Agra Road is the only truck terminal in the study area due
to which the on-street parking of trucks along the regional connectivity roads, bypass
roads and along access roads of various industrial areas has aggregated over the years
leading to traffic snarls and congestion. The roads that witness maximum on-street
parking are Delhi Bypass, Tonk Road, Sikar Road, Gopalpura Bypass, Agra Road, Ajmer
Road etc. only. Therefore, it is essential to develop truck terminals in the study area at
the earliest.
There is an intermixing of freight and local traffic in the city. As an underlying principle,
CMP proposes complete segregation of freight and local traffic by locating freight
terminals at the periphery of the city (direction-oriented freight terminals). The truck
terminal locations are proposed at the outskirts of the study area along the cordon
roads so that the unnecessary truck movement for parking is avoided within major road
network of the study area. Further, the truck terminals are proposed before the
proposed ring road alignment so that the trucks can directly access the ring road
without entering the core part of the study area.
The four locations have been proposed for the development of freight/ truck terminals.

4.8.4. Junction Improvement Measures
Traffic congestion is a growing challenge in Jaipur and needs to be addressed through a
range of traffic management interventions. At present, traffic control measures are
minimal, with most of the signalized junctions being non-functional. A large number of
junctions remain uncontrolled, which is a major cause of congestion, particularly in the
city’s core area. Several key junctions that cater to heavy traffic volumes suffer from
faulty geometry and lack of proper traffic control mechanisms. These junctions have
been identified for improvement through geometric redesign and introduction of
appropriate traffic management measures.
To enhance efficiency and safety, the following measures are suggested:
• Traffic Signal Upgradation:
o Reactivate and modernize traffic signals with adaptive/area traffic control
systems.
o Introduce pedestrian phases in the signal cycle.
o Integrate signals with Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) for coordinated
corridor management.
• Rotary Geometry Improvements:
o Reduce excessive rotary diameters (where feasible) to improve deflection and
reduce high-speed weaving.
o Modify entry and exit radii to conform to IRC standards, ensuring smoother
merging and diverging movements.
o Introduce channelizing islands to separate turning movements and guide
vehicles.
• Median Realignment:
o Remove or realign protruding medians that obstruct entry/exit movements.
o Provide uniform median noses with proper end treatment for safety.

o Ensure median openings are rationalized and restricted to planned movements
only.
• Pedestrian Safety Measures:
o Provide zebra crossings at entry and exit arms with refuge islands.
o Grade-separated crossings (FOBs/subways) may be considered at high
pedestrian volume rotaries.
o Introduce tactile paving, ramps, and adequate lighting for universal accessibility.
• Traffic Calming & Safety Enhancements:
o Use speed calming measures at rotary approaches (rumble strips, markings).
o Improve visibility with advance warning signage, retro-reflective markings, and

o Provide guard rails/barriers at pedestrian crossing points to channel safe

• Public Transport Integration:

o Introduce CCTV monitoring linked to the Integrated Command & Control Centre
(ICCC).
o Ensure regular maintenance of signals, signage, and markings.
• Split Cycle Offset Optimization Technique (SCOOT)
SCOOT is a tool for managing and controlling traffic signals in urban areas. It is an
adaptive system that responds automatically to fluctuations in traffic flow through the
use of on-street detectors embedded in the road. This system typically reduces traffic
delay by an average of 20% in urban areas. Apart from this, SCOOT also contains other
traffic management facilities such as:
o Bus priority
o Traffic gating
o Incident detection
o On-line saturation occupancy measurement
o Vehicle emissions estimates
SCOOT based traffic management is recommended for all mobility corridors in the city.

4.10.1. Regulatory Measures
Limited road capacity, increasing vehicle ownership and limited penetration of public
transport are the main reasons for the present chaotic traffic scenario in the city. The
following regulatory measures are required to bring in improvements in the present
scenario.
a. Transport Demand Management
Transportation Demand Management or TDM refers to various strategies that change
travel behavior (how, when and where people travel) in order to increase transport
system efficiency and achieve specific objectives such as reduced traffic congestion,
increased safety, improved mobility for non-drivers, energy conservation and pollution
emission reductions. TABLE 4.26 gives the TDM Measures used worldwide to manage
the transport demand in the cities.

i. Park and Ride and PT Promotion
Park & Ride facilities and promotion of public transport are the key components of the
strategy adopted to meet the demand in horizon years. Public transport promotion
needs to be carried out through policy interventions as well as awareness programs.
The mass transport system plan detailed in previous sections will promote public

ii. Preferential HOV Parking and Carpool Promotion and Coordination
Preferential HOV parking and carpool promotion and coordination provide
opportunities for socializing and reduce commute times through the usage of dedicated
carpool lanes. The designation of premium parking spaces for High Occupancy Vehicles
(HOV) modes is an inexpensive way to encourage employees to carpool or vanpool. It is
intended to make HOV spaces highly valued among employees over single occupant
vehicle spaces. The priority spaces are located close to the building entrances to reduce
the walk time for carpool and vanpool users. Reduced walk times yield a relative
reduction of travel times for HOV users. In addition to demonstrating employer support
for HOV commuting, preferential HOV parking may also reduce the demand for
employee parking spaces. Parking permit fees may also be waived or reduced for HOVs
as an added incentive.
Carpool promotion and coordination is successful when implemented by employers
because they can efficiently market the programs at the workplace and provide
matching functions based on employer records. As employees commute from areas

further away from employment centers to buy affordable housing, vanpools become
increasingly attractive as a means to reduce single-occupant trips.
iii. Alternative Measures
Alternative work-hour programs offered by individual employers such as the
compressed work week, flexi time, and telecommuting are TDM strategies that directly
reduce the number of trips taken by employees to travel to work.
A compressed work week allows employees to work longer days in exchange for an
additional day off that would normally be worked. For example, employees may work
eight nine-hour days and one eight-hour day, in a 10-day (2-week) pay period, totaling
80 hours and permitting one day off each two weeks. In other cases, employees may
work four ten-hour days each week, with one day off each week. This program not only
reduces the amount of peak hour commute trips, but also is often attractive to
employees, increasing morale and job satisfaction.
Other strategies such as “flexi time” or staggered work hours can be used to reduce
peak hour trips and spread trips throughout non-peak times by allowing employees to
begin and end work at a time that is different from the typical 9 A.M. to 6 P.M. work
schedule. Flexi work time can be particularly attractive to employees with commutes
that are congested during peak times, but do not result in the elimination of daily trips
in the manner achieved by the compressed work week strategy.
All over the world, cities have adopted TDM measures to control congestion and
promote public transport. The lessons learnt from the experience suggest that TDM
should be sold as a part of an overall transport strategy. The public has to see the big
picture. TDM is only one part of a package of measures, which included others like
building roads, sophisticated traffic management, priority for bus movements, and new
rail system. All the parts of the package need to be done in parallel to get the desired
result.
b. Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Policy – Rajasthan (2025)
The Government of Rajasthan has notified the Transit Oriented Development (TOD)
Policy, 2025 to promote compact, mixed-use, and transit-supportive urban
development along major public transport corridors. The policy seeks to integrate land-
use and transport planning to increase public transport ridership, reduce reliance on
private vehicles, optimise infrastructure investments, and enable sustainable and
efficient urban growth.
Under the policy, TOD influence zones are delineated within walkable catchments of
mass transit facilities such as metro stations, railway stations and other high-capacity
public transport systems. These zones are envisaged as high-density, pedestrian-
February 2026 Page 4-82
Comprehensive Mobility Plan for Jaipur City
Draft CMP Chapter 4: Development of Comprehensive Mobility Plan
oriented areas supporting a balanced mix of residential, commercial, institutional, and
recreational uses, thereby enabling shorter trip lengths and enhanced access to daily
activities through public transport.
A key aspect of the policy is the provision of development incentives, including
enhanced FAR/FSI and flexible land-use provisions, subject to compliance with
prescribed urban design, access, and infrastructure norms. The policy encourages
reduced parking standards within TOD zones to discourage private vehicle use and
promote modal shift towards public transport, walking, and cycling. Strong emphasis is
placed on Non-Motorised Transport (NMT) infrastructure, including wide and
continuous footpaths, universal accessibility, active street frontage, and safe last-mile
connectivity to transit stations.
The TOD Policy mandates integration with statutory planning instruments such as
Master Plans, Development Plans, and Comprehensive Mobility Plans (CMPs), ensuring
that transit investments are supported by appropriate land-use planning. Development
authorities are required to identify TOD nodes, prepare area-specific TOD plans, and
enable coordinated implementation through close collaboration among urban local
bodies, transport agencies, and infrastructure providers. Institutionally, the policy
encourages the creation of dedicated TOD cells or nodal agencies to facilitate approvals,
inter-departmental coordination, and monitoring of TOD initiatives. Implementation is
largely market-driven, allowing voluntary participation by landowners and developers
while adhering to prescribed planning and design standards.
The policy provides a clear implementation framework through TOD Schemes, classified
as Category-1 (up to 1 ha) and Category-2 (1 ha and above) based on scheme area.
Category-1 schemes must be entirely located within the Intense Development Area
(IDA) of a TOD node, where mixed use is permitted but not mandatory. Category-2
schemes may partially or fully fall within the IDA; however, mixed use is mandatory
across the entire scheme, with at least 25% of the area within the IDA and full inclusion
within the TOD Planning Area. All TOD schemes are required to have access from an
existing road with a minimum Right of Way (ROW) of 18 m, and provisions are made for
plot amalgamation and reconstitution to facilitate integrated and comprehensive
development.
The policy prescribes mixed-use distribution and development intensity through
defined Built-up Area Ratio (BAR) norms based on existing land use and scheme
category. A balanced mix of residential, commercial, and public/semi-public uses is
ensured, while retaining minimum proportions of the original land use. The required
mix may be achieved either horizontally across plots or vertically within buildings,
subject to compatibility and safety considerations. BAR for a TOD scheme is calculated
as the aggregate of BAR entitlements of all constituent plots. For both Category-1 and
Category-2 schemes, the base BAR is as per prevailing Building Bye-laws, with an
enhanced TOD BAR of up to 3.0, subject to a minimum ROW of 12 m. Building height is

4.11. DEVELOPMENT OF FISCAL MEASURES
4.11.1. Fare Policy for Public Transport
a. Principles for Rational Public Transport Tariff Design
Public transport tariff design is the key for creating an enabling environment for
dynamic and sustainable growth of public transport sector. The fundamental principle
of tariff determination is to ensure that prices lead to an optimum level of investment,
operation, and demand in the sector.
Generally, there is a conflict between the different objectives of fare. For example, to
increase the share of public transport and addressing issues of social sustainability
require that the fares be kept sufficiently low, while efficiency improvement and
viability issues require periodic fare increases with the increase in cost of input of the
service. The agencies in this sector need to balance these objectives to achieve a
sustainable outcome. Similarly, to ensure environmental and social sustainability, it may
be necessary to subsidize public transport operations.
b. Effect on Demand of Bus Services
An increase in public transport fares could lead to modal shift to private modes. Thus,
public transport fares would have to be benchmarked on the cost of alternative modes
of transport to ensure that a modal shift is checked. For addressing issues of social
sustainability, it is imperative that the fares be kept sufficiently low. However, tariffs
should provide incentives for efficiency improvements so as to reduce the cost of
operation.
c. Subsidy Administration

e. Integrated Ticketing and Fare Management Systems
To enable seamless, integrated, and user-friendly urban mobility in Jaipur, it is proposed
the implementation of a Unified Mobility Card (UMC) across the city’s public transport
and allied mobility services. The UMC shall serve as a single, interoperable, and cashless
payment instrument for passengers, reducing dependency on multiple tickets and
payment systems.
The proposed UMC shall be aligned with the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC –
One Nation, One Card) framework and shall be implemented through coordinated
efforts of Jaipur Metro Rail Corporation (JMRC) and Jaipur City Transport Services
Limited (JCTSL). The card shall enable seamless travel across Jaipur Metro services
operated by JMRC and city bus services operated by JCTSL, with future integration of
suburban rail services, parking facilities, and other mobility-related services.
Implementation of the UMC is expected to significantly reduce transaction time at
ticketing counters, minimize queuing during peak hours, and improve passenger
convenience and accessibility. The system will support online recharge facilities, mobile-
based integration, and multiple fare products, including passes and time-based tickets,
thereby improving operational efficiency and ridership experience.
The UMC will also facilitate data-driven transport planning and operations, providing
valuable insights into passenger travel patterns, peak demand periods, and modal
interchange behavior. Such data shall support service optimization, rush management
strategies, fare integration and revisions, and capacity planning for public transport.
Phased implementation approach is recommended, with initial deployment across
Jaipur Metro and city bus services, followed by expansion to parking management, park-
and-ride facilities, and other urban transport services
4.11.2. Parking Pricing Strategy
The land in urban areas is limited and there is a limit to the parking space that can be
created in the city. The parking demand is growing with growth of vehicles in Jaipur. The
institutional, public semipublic and busy/commercial areas are major attractors to the
long-term parking. This results in the vehicle parking spilling to streets (main roads or
side streets). One of the important tools to control parking is Parking Pricing. This may
include following measures:
• Levy incremental parking fee on on-street parking
• Off street parking charges to be less than the on-street parking charges

a. Parking Pricing for Core Area
It is proposed to levy incremental parking charges upon on-street parking in the areas

b. Parking Pricing for Area beyond Core Area
Parking pricing for areas beyond core area is proposed to be lower than that of areas
inside the core area. Higher parking charges for internal areas will reduce parking
demand in these congested areas. Similar to parking pricing strategy for internal areas,
short-term parking is promoted for areas beyond core area as compared to long-term
parking by incremental pricing for high rate of parking turnovers.

As parking is unsatiated demand, it is proposed that regulatory tools need to be adopted
to cater parking demand generated by a building inside its own premises. This will cater

5.4.1. Implementation Mechanism
The possible areas of the urban transport projects for various implementation
agencies are presented in Table 5.4. Low capital intensive with moderate technical
requirements and high social responsibility projects can be taken up by ULBs. High
capital intensive and more technical required projects like High-Capacity Bus System
and structural projects shall be through the co-operation of State and Central
governments on SPV format with loan from multilateral funding agencies. Projects
with overlapping responsibilities but with high return potentials with less risk and
less gestation period shall be through private sector by BOT/Annuity formats. Private
sector participation will be in the areas of high profitability with less/medium risks.
Hence it is necessary to identify the appropriate areas for different types of private
sector participation for implementing urban transport components. Private sector
involvement in urban transport components can be in following forms:
• Projects with social responsibility on sponsorship pattern (eg: improvement and
maintenance of junctions).
• Annuity format of BOT projects which have less return potentials and high capital
intensive (e.g. Development and maintenance of City Roads in Trivandrum City).
• Commercial projects BOT projects (e.g. Coimbatore Bypass in Tamil Nadu, Bridge
connecting Wellington Island and Mattancherry in Kochi in Kerala).
• PPP for urban bus services (e.g. AICTSL for Indore city bus operation for the bus
services proposed for the Study Area)
5.4.2. Funding Models for Projects Implementation
• Metro system
The financing option for Metro implementation depends upon selection of the
dedicated agency created to implement the project. As per Metro Rail Policy, 2017,
the prominent models are:
o Equity Sharing Model – Special Purpose Vehicle fully under Government
Control: Under this arrangement Government of India and State
Government make equal equity contribution and run SPV as a commercial
enterprise. As per the prevalent practice, Central Government contributes
20% of the project cost as their equity contribution. An equal amount can be

• Development of Terminals (Bus/Freight)
The development of bus and freight terminals may be undertaken through suitable
Public–Private Partnership (PPP) frameworks to ensure efficient delivery, optimal
risk sharing, and long-term operational sustainability. Among the commonly adopted
PPP models are:
o Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) model, wherein the public
authority retains responsibility for financing and operations
o Build–Operate–Transfer (BOT) model, which involves private sector
participation in construction and operation for a defined concession period;
o Design–Build–Finance–Operate–Transfer (DBFOT) model.
The DBFOT model is generally preferred for terminal development, as it integrates
design, construction, financing, and operations under a single concessionaire,
promotes innovation and efficiency, and reduces lifecycle costs while ensuring
improved service quality and asset maintenance over the concession period.
• Development of Multilevel Parking and Public Bike Sharing
The development of multilevel parking facilities may be undertaken through
appropriate Public–Private Partnership (PPP) models to address urban parking
demand in an efficient and financially viable manner. Commonly adopted models
include the EPC model, wherein construction is carried out by a private contractor
with public funding and subsequent operation by the authority, and the Build–
Operate–Transfer (BOT) model. The BOT model is generally preferred for multilevel
parking projects, as it enables private sector participation in financing, construction,
and operation, ensures better asset management during the concession period, and
reduces the financial burden on the public authority.
• Development of Public Bike Sharing
Public Bike Sharing (PBS) systems are typically implemented through a hybrid PPP
model, combining public support in the form of Viability Gap Funding (VGF) with
private sector participation in operations and maintenance. Under this model, the
public authority supports initial capital expenditure and system rollout, while the
private operator is responsible for day-to-day operations, maintenance, and service
quality. This approach has been widely adopted, as it ensures financial sustainability,
operational efficiency, and scalability of the bike-sharing system while promoting
non-motorized and sustainable urban mobility

5.4.3. Indirect sources for funding Urban Transport infrastructure
A number of reports by various organizations have drawn attention to the indirect
values created by transportation projects, suggesting that these could be tapped for
potential funding of the projects themselves. Among the indirect benefits identified in
these reports, the two most important are:
Transit Oriented Development and Land Value Capture: Investments in urban
transport lead to higher property values in developed areas (and to higher municipal
rates linked to those properties), to greater orientation of development along transit
directions, to better anchors for land use planning, etc. Not only do private property
owners gain indirectly from higher values of their holdings around new infrastructure,
sometimes their rights to develop their properties are also gifted freely by cities and
transit systems hoping to boost ridership.
According to various studies, the value is estimated at between 5% - 10% for
residential properties, and between 10% - 30% for commercial properties. To generate
funding from the value created in the proximity zones, a ‘Betterment Levy’ or ‘Land
Value Tax’ can be imposed. This tax is aimed at landowners as it focuses on land value
rather than property value. The tax is designed to capture the value created by the
provision of public services surrounding the areas in which the services have been
provisioned.
Revenue estimation investigates and assesses the potential revenue generation that
may be derived from the transit-oriented development planning initiatives along the
high-capacity bus corridor through various value capture techniques. Revenue from
TOD planning initiatives may be generated through various ways like sale of additional
FSI, revenue from stamp duty, property tax, sale of premium towards ancillaries,
development charges etc.
Property development is the key factor in determining success of a High-Capacity Bus
system. Evidence continues to mount that transit can generate tremendous value by
concentrating development and activity around stations, and that this value can be
captured and used to fund station area improvements and community benefits.
Process of property development requires land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and
management as major inputs.
Development Rights granted by cities to the areas near the transportation project,
either at very low cost to owners or in some cases free. These benefits could instead
be held in escrow by the transport project itself and made available to property
owners on a paid basis, with the money earned through such transactions available to
under-write a portion of the project costs.

Fuel Cess: Another source of income is from private vehicles through taxes levied on
their consumption of fuel. Typically, cities can add taxes or cess applicable within their
jurisdiction, collecting money for use in making improvements to public transport
schemes. Given the rising use of private vehicles, and the large amounts of money that
can be collected by even a small cess on fuel purchases, this could be an important
source of money for cities.
Urban Transport Tax: Urban Transport Tax or Cess may be levied on the purchase of
new cars and two wheelers.
Carbon Credits: Another source of funds that has emerged in recent years is carbon
credits, typically traded between industrialized countries that operate at high levels of
per-capita pollution, and less industrialized economies where the per-capita climate
impacts are much smaller. In the short run, these credits allow richer economies to
phase out their shift from carbon-intensive production, and also allow poorer
countries to source funds for their project needs. Credits are also available for
countries’ willingness to choose less carbon-intensive choices for their own industries,
and some Indian entities (e.g. bus operators in some states) are examining ways of
seeking such credits for the use of biodiesel in their vehicles. However, the overall
trading scenario around such credits is full of uncertainty and is likely to be
determined by global climate talks. Wherever they are available, however, they can be
tapped to augment other sources of funds.
Unified Mobility Card (UMC): The Unified Mobility Card (UMC) presents significant
opportunities for generating non-fare revenue while strengthening integrated urban
mobility in Jaipur. Revenue can be generated through partnerships with banks and
financial institutions for card issuance, co-branding, and revenue sharing on
transaction fees. The UMC ecosystem also enables float income from stored-value
balances, interest earnings, and settlement efficiencies. Additional revenue streams
may be realized through merchant integrations, allowing the card to be used for
parking, retail outlets, last-mile services, and civic amenities, with a share of
transaction commissions accruing to the implementing agencies. Advertising and
branding rights on physical cards, mobile applications, and associated infrastructure
further provide monetization opportunities.
EV Charging and Battery Swapping Stations: Electric vehicle (EV) charging and battery
swapping infrastructure offers multiple direct revenue opportunities through user-
based charges such as pay-per-use tariffs (per kWh or time-based), per-swap fees, and
subscription or leasing models for commercial fleets including e-buses, e-autos, taxis,
and last-mile delivery vehicles. Battery swapping, in particular, enables predictable
and recurring revenue due to high utilization by fleet operators. Public agencies can
further monetize these facilities through PPP or concession models, wherein private
operators invest, operate, and share revenues via license fees, fixed annuities, or

revenue-sharing mechanisms. In addition, ancillary and indirect revenue streams, such
as land monetization at depots, terminals, parking areas, and transit hubs through
leasing space for charging equipment and allied infrastructure, can significantly
enhance financial viability.
Urban Transport Fund (UTF): As recommended in the NUTP, states and cities are
being encouraged to set up UTFs in order to receive dedicated revenues to be used
exclusively for meeting the needs of urban transport. The NUTP mentions some of the
potential revenue sources for such UTFs, which include a supplement to the petrol and
diesel taxes, a betterment levy on landowners, and tax on employers etc.
Four options for geographical coverage of an UTF have been identified: UTF at the
state level for the whole state; UTF for a particular municipal / urban area; UTF at the
state level for urban areas that do not have their own UTF or UTF for UMTA
jurisdiction.
There are multiple advantages of having UTF at municipal / urban area level. One is
that the funds are specifically available for meeting the urban transport needs of a
single city. Another is that the amount of funding is better known at the local level
than at the state level and therefore a UTF at a municipal / urban area will allow for
better planning. Third is that the use of the funds can better be prioritised according
to the local needs. Since it is envisaged that UMTA should be established at municipal
levels, the preferred option is to have UTF with jurisdiction similar to UMTA
jurisdiction.
Different sources of funds have been identified by different states while setting up
UTFs. In most of the UTFs, a major source of funding is from the Government. This has
taken different forms such as budgetary allocations, government grants, grants
through schemes etc. Several other sources of funds have been identified to
supplement funding from government resources.
Some of these sources of funds are common across various UTFs while others are less
common. For example, cess on vehicle registration is used as a common source of
funding in many of the UTFs. Similarly, betterment levy (which is also a suggested
source of fund in the NUTP) is one of the common sources in some of the UTFs. An
example of a less common source of funding is a premium charged on Transfer of
Development Rights (TDR) which is used by Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation.
In some of the UTFs, there are provisions of receiving funds from international funding
agencies such as World Bank, ADB etc.

Currently, at this road elevated Metro alignment goes underground before reaching

falls on station road, encroachment and unorganized parking create congestion. (
Three lane 9 m wide road is basically used for the entry/ exit of the Sindhi camp terminal,
and rest of the available width is encroached by the private bus booking counters, shops,
stalls, auto-rickshaws and people walking on the road (
on the road does not provide sufficient turning radius for the vehicles at the median cut
due to which traffic chaos can be observed along the road.
No designated and organized parking is available for IPTs and private vehicles
outside the terminal which results in on-street parking of IPTs and private
vehicles. The on-street parking reduces the effective carriageway capacity of the
Vehicles have to turn from the median gap to enter the terminal which creates a
conflict point with the existing road traffic and during peak time, they completely
stall the traffic as shown in
Footpaths are not available for the pedestrian movement alongside the road. Jay
walking is observed due to absence of pedestrian crossing facilities (
One entry/ exit gate of the Metro is opening inside Sindhi camp terminal and other
one is on the other side of the abutting road which results in heavy pedestrian
crossing movement and pedestrian – vehicle conflicts.
The circulation within Sindhi Camp Bus terminal is proposed to be made clockwise for a
better circulation with the abutting road which will overcome the conflicts. By shifting
the entry and exit points, circulation will be improved.

Press Release:Press Information Bureau
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways
Year End Review 2023-Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
National Highway (NH) network increased by 60% from 91,287 km in 2014 to 1,46,145 km in year 2023
Length of 4 lanes and above NH increased by 2.5 times – 18,387 km (2014) to 46,179 km (Nov’23)
Length of less than 2 lane NH decreased from 30% (2014) to 10% (Nov’23)
Average pace of NH construction increased by 143% to 28.3 km/day from 2014
Expenditure is expected to increase by 9.4 times to Rs 3.17 lakh Crore from 2014
Out of 108 (3700 km) port connectivity road projects, 8 (294 km) are completed, 28 (1808 km) are awarded and DPR under-progress for 72 (1595 km) projects
100% achievement of Special Campaign 3.0 from 02.10.2023 to 31.10.2023
Bharat New Car Assessment Programme  launched for safety rating of passenger cars and empowering consumers to take informed decisions
49,770 Vehicles Scrapped till date under Vehicle Scrapping Policy -44 RVSFs are operational across 15 States and 37 ATSs operationalized across 8 States
2 mobile application -Rajmarg Yatra – Customer Redressal system and NHAI One – Digital tool for on site NH project execution launched
Relief measures for Contractors/Developers of the Road Sector in view of the COVID-19 Pandemic extended till 31st March’24
Vahan and Sarathi  implemented in all RTOs of 35 States/UTs (Except Telangana)

A. NATIONAL HIGHWAYS: CONSTRUCTION & ACHIEVEMENTS
1. Road Network in the Country:
India has about 66.71 lakh km of road network, which is the second largest in the world.
The length of various categories of roads is as under:
National Highways: 1,46,145 km
State Highways: 1,79,535 km
Other Roads: 63,45,403 km
National Highways play a very important role in the economic and social development of the country by enabling efficient movement of freight and passengers and improving access to markets. MoRTH and its implementing agencies have undertaken multiple initiatives in last 9 years to augment the capacity of the National Highway infrastructure in India.
2. National Highway Network

2. Bharatmala Pariyojana:
The Bharatmala Pariyojana was launched with the primary focus on optimizing the efficiency of the movement of goods and people across the country. Phase I of the Bharatmala Pariyojana approved in October 2017, focuses on bridging critical infrastructure gaps through development of 34,800 km of National Highways. The Pariyojana emphasised a “corridor based National Highway development” to ensure infrastructure symmetry and consistent road user experience. The key components of the Pariyojana are Economic Corridors development, Inter-corridor and feeder routes development, National Corridors Efficiency Improvement, Border, and International Connectivity Roads, Coastal and Port Connectivity Roads and Expressways.
Status of Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase 1:
The status of Bharatmala Pariyojana Phase 1 entails a total length of 34,800 km in 31 States and UTs, 550+ Districts. The length awarded is 27,384 km and the length constructed is 15,045 km.
The phase 1 is to be completed by 27-28.
3.
Relief for Contractors/Developers of the Road Sector in view of the COVID-19 Pandemic:
The Ministry provided/extended the relief measures in view of the Covid-19 pandemic:
(i)
Extension of relaxation in Schedule H/G till 31
st
March 2024
to improve the liquidity of funds available with the Contractors and Concessionaire.
(ii)
Arrangement regarding direct payment to approved Sub-Contractor
through Escrow Account may be continued
till 31
st
March
2024
or the completion of the work by the Sub-Contractor, whichever is earlier.
(iii)
Reduction of Performance Security/release of retention money
: Reduction of Performance Security/release of retention money: This Ministry has already decided to reduce Performance Security from existing 5–10 % to 3% of the value of the contract for all existing contracts (excluding the contracts under dispute wherein arbitration/court proceedings have already been started or are completed). All tenders/contracts issued/ concluded till 31.03.2024 should also have the provision of reduced performance security. However, in order to ensure the quality of work being executed, the Ministry will advise all project executing agencies to ensure that in case of abnormally low bids (ALBs), additional performance security is realized as per the latest guidelines provided by the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of finance. Retention money is a part of the Performance Security till the construction period. Hence, the release of retention money may be continued in proportion to the work already executed and no reduction of retention money may be made from the Bills raised by the Contractor till 31.03.2024.
For HAM/BOT Contracts, a Performance Guarantee may be released on a pro-rata basis, as provided in the Contract if Concessionaire is not in breach of the Contract.
Changes in the Model Concessionaire Agreement (MCA) & Request for Proposal (RFP) of the road construction models: -
(i)
Change in MCA for HAM projects to allow for flexible pavement including structures. Changes have been made in the RFP and MCA of HAM project to allow Lowest Quoted Bid Project Cost (BPC) as the basis for awarding HAM Project and cost to be fixed as in EPC projects. The changes in Clause 23.7 of MCA of HAM project issued by MoRTH included following three categories:
a) For flexible perpetual pavement including structures
b) For rigid pavement with 10-year maintenance period including structures
c) For stand-alone Bridges/Tunnel works
(ii)
Inclusions of provisions regarding accepting Insurance Surety Bonds and e-bank guarantee as “Bid Security and Performance Security” in standard documents of EPC, HAM, and BOT (Toll):
Department of Expenditure vide Office Memorandum No. F. 1/4/2022-PPD dated 05.08.2022 made amendments in the Rule 170(i) and Rule 171(i) of General Financial Rules (GFR), 2017 to include e-bank guarantee as a means to accept Bid Security and Performance Security. Further, Department of Expenditure had amended Rule 170 (i) and Rule 171 (i) of GFR, 2017 to accept provision of Insurance Surety Bond as a mean of ‘Bid.
Security’ and ‘Performance Security’ vide OM dated 02.02.2022. The latest Circular issued by Department of Expenditure, O.M No. F. 1/2/2023- PPD dated 03.04.2023, also provides for Insurance Surety Bonds and e-bank guarantee as possible means of furnishing Performance Security. In view of this, necessary amendments were made in the standard documents of EPC, HAM, and BoT (Toll) by the Ministry.
4. Asset Monetization:
TOT Model – Under this model, the right of collection of user fee (toll) in respect of selected operational highways constructed through public funding are assigned through a concession agreement as a result of bidding. For a specified period of 15-30 years to the Concessionaire against upfront payment of a lump-sum amount quoted to the Government/NHAI. During the concession period, the responsibility for operations and maintenance of the road assets rests with the Concessionaire. Since its launch in 2018, NHAI has successfully completed 6 rounds of the Road Asset (bundle of roads) of monetization through TOT mode and raised Rs. 26,366 crores. LoAs are issued under ToT bundles 11, 12, 13 & 14 and realization of Rs 15,968 Cr concession fee is expected in FY 2023-24. It is also pertinent to mention here that LoAs for these 4 TOT Bundles were issued by NHAI within one day of opening of the respective Financial bids.  Total asset monetization under this model is expected to be Rs 42,334 Cr by the end of FY 2023-24.
InVIT Model – NHAI has set up an InvIT under the SEBI InvIT Regulations, 2014, in which NHAI is having 16% stake apart from main investors (CPPIB, OTPP etc.). InvIT is a pooled investment vehicle that issues units to investors, while having three entities for management of the Trust – Trustee, Investment Manager and Project Manager. The three entities have defined roles and responsibilities under the SEBI Regulations. Two rounds (635 km) were taken up and finalised. Under this model, concession fee of Rs.10,200 crores has been realized so far.  Rs.15,000 crore is expected to be realized in FY 2023-24 through another round.
Securitization through SPV Model – A SPV/DME (100% owned by NHAI), has been created by bundling road assets under consideration and securitizing the future user fee from the road assets. NHAI will collect tolls, maintain the road assets and periodically transfer payments to the SPV sufficient for servicing debt obligations at the SPV level. About Rs.37,000 crore has already been raised through this method (DME- Delhi Mumbai Expressway) by NHAI so far. Another, Rs.6,000 crore is expected to be raised under this model in FY 2023-24.

These road projects will be developed at a total cost of about Rs 6400 crores. ROAD TRANSPORT
Road transport is the dominant mode of transport in India, both in terms of traffic share and contribution to the national economy. Apart from facilitating the movement of goods and passengers, road transport plays a key role in promoting equitable socio-economic development across regions of the country. It also plays a vital role in social and economic integration and development of the country. Easy accessibility, flexibility of operations, door-to-door service and reliability have earned road transport a greater significance in both passenger and freight traffic vis-à-vis other modes of transport.

rd

Real Driving Emission (RDE) Regulations: -
There is a gap in the emission performance when the same vehicle is tested in laboratory conditions and in real driving conditions. To reduce this gap, Real Driving Emission (RDE) regulations were introduced in Europe. In line with this, India also introduced RDE regulations along with the introduction of Bharat Stage VI (BS VI), making RDE measurement mandatory during type approval and COP. The said regulations are applicable from 1
st
April 2020 for data collection and from 1
st
April, 2023 for meeting Conformity factor (CF). CF defines the emission limits of the RDE regulations.
The Ministry of Road transport and Highways has mandated that the CF (conformity Factor) may be applicable, in respect of vehicles manufactured on and after 1
st
April, 2023 for all vehicles on real world driving cycle emission.
All-India Tourist Permit Rules, 2023: -
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has notified the All-India Tourist Vehicles (Permit) Rules, 2023, superseding the All-India Tourist Vehicle (Authorization or Permit) Rules, 2021.
The rules notified in 2021 had provided a significant boost to the tourism sector in India by streamlining and simplifying the permit regime for tourist vehicles.
Now, with the All-India Tourist Vehicles (Permit) Rules, 2023, the All-India Tourist Permit (AITP) regime has been further streamlined and strengthened to provide greater ease of movement of tourist vehicles across the country.
The key features of the new rules are as follows:
a.       To simplify the application procedure and to reduce compliance burden, the provision of authorization and AITP have been made independent of each other.
b.       To promote deployment of electric vehicles and vehicles driven on methanol or ethanol fuel in large numbers, a streamlined regulatory ecosystem at no cost to the operator(s) has been introduced.
c.       More categories of tourist vehicles, with lesser permit fees for lesser capacity vehicles (less than ten) have been introduced. This is expected to provide considerable financial relief to smaller tourist vehicle operators, having smaller vehicles with lower seating capacity, as they will now be required to pay lower fees commensurate with the seating capacity of their vehicle(s).

This Ministry had extended the scope of AIS 135 from the engine compartment to include the passenger compartment of school buses and buses of Type III category amending CMVR for incorporating provision for fire protection of the passenger compartment of the buses. The implementation timeline was twelve months from the date of commencement of the Central Motor Vehicles (First Amendment) Rules, i.e. from 27
th
January 2023. The aim of this amendment is to provide an additional evacuation time to the occupants and thus to enhance the safety in fire incidents in buses through FPS and FAS. The standard was framed in consultation with various stakeholders including the experts of DRDO which had undertaken the design and had also tested the concept on a bus.
After receiving the representation from automotive stakeholders, this Ministry has deferred the date of implementation to 1
st
