4.6.4. Proposed Freight Terminals
The presence of various RIICO industries and Kanakpura Dry Port results in generation
of substantial amount of freight traffic. Further, Jaipur Region falls in between the busy
corridor connecting Delhi and Mumbai. The timely and smooth movement of such
freight is crucial to the well-being of the people and the viability of the economic
activities they undertake. Considerable goods movement is observed along major
highways like NH-48, NH-52, NH-21, NH-248, SH-12, SH-2C, and SH-55. However, the
entry of heavy vehicles to the core city has been restricted during the daytime and is
allowed only during late night hours (11 pm to 4 am).
Transport Nagar located on Agra Road is the only truck terminal in the study area due
to which the on-street parking of trucks along the regional connectivity roads, bypass
roads and along access roads of various industrial areas has aggregated over the years
leading to traffic snarls and congestion. The roads that witness maximum on-street
parking are Delhi Bypass, Tonk Road, Sikar Road, Gopalpura Bypass, Agra Road, Ajmer
Road etc. only. Therefore, it is essential to develop truck terminals in the study area at
the earliest.
There is an intermixing of freight and local traffic in the city. As an underlying principle,
CMP proposes complete segregation of freight and local traffic by locating freight
terminals at the periphery of the city (direction-oriented freight terminals). The truck
terminal locations are proposed at the outskirts of the study area along the cordon
roads so that the unnecessary truck movement for parking is avoided within major road
network of the study area. Further, the truck terminals are proposed before the
proposed ring road alignment so that the trucks can directly access the ring road
without entering the core part of the study area.
The four locations have been proposed for the development of freight/ truck terminals.
There is a proposal of Transport Nagar on Sikar Road near Todi which is in planning

Retail and wholesale commercial activities are spread all over the core area. These
activities need to be accessed not only by the buyers but also by the supply chain.
Besides, the goods purchased also need to be moved from the core. The said processes
require goods vehicles such as LCVs and Trucks to access the core area. As these vehicles
need to be parked in and around core area, even after removal of on street parking of
private vehicles, the problem of congestion will persist.
Thus, it is proposed here to restrict the entrance of Trucks in the core area during
daytime i.e. from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. All the goods transfer from and to the Core area
shall be taken up during the night hours when passenger movement in the Core is
minimal.
To manage freight efficiently and minimize traffic disruptions, provision of designated
truck lay-bys is proposed. Truck lay-bys are planned at strategic locations along major
arterial roads, city entry points, ring road corridors, and near industrial areas to
facilitate short-term halting, rest, and compliance with time-based entry regulations.
The lay-bys shall be designed as per applicable IRC guidelines, with adequate entry–exit
tapers, pavement strength for heavy loads, lighting, signage, and basic amenities, while
parking space planning shall follow URDPFI norms. The proposed lay-bys at New
Transport Nagar, Kanakpura, Bagru, Mahindra SEZ are shown in FIGURE 4.29.
Goods transaction in Core during daytime is proposed to take place by IPT. The goods
IPT vehicles will also pay on street and off-street parking charges. Though, a goods
vehicle will not be allowed to be parked on the street for more than 2 hours duration.
Long term goods IPT parking shall be only done on off street parking complexes.

4.8.4. Junction Improvement Measures
Traffic congestion is a growing challenge in Jaipur and needs to be addressed through a
range of traffic management interventions. At present, traffic control measures are
minimal, with most of the signalized junctions being non-functional. A large number of
junctions remain uncontrolled, which is a major cause of congestion, particularly in the
city’s core area. Several key junctions that cater to heavy traffic volumes suffer from
faulty geometry and lack of proper traffic control mechanisms. These junctions have
been identified for improvement through geometric redesign and introduction of
appropriate traffic management measures.
To enhance efficiency and safety, the following measures are suggested:
• Traffic Signal Upgradation:
o Reactivate and modernize traffic signals with adaptive/area traffic control
systems.
o Introduce pedestrian phases in the signal cycle.
o Integrate signals with Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS) for coordinated
corridor management.
• Rotary Geometry Improvements:
o Reduce excessive rotary diameters (where feasible) to improve deflection and
reduce high-speed weaving.
o Modify entry and exit radii to conform to IRC standards, ensuring smoother
merging and diverging movements.
o Introduce channelizing islands to separate turning movements and guide
vehicles.
• Median Realignment:
o Remove or realign protruding medians that obstruct entry/exit movements.
o Provide uniform median noses with proper end treatment for safety.

o Ensure median openings are rationalized and restricted to planned movements
only.
• Pedestrian Safety Measures:
o Provide zebra crossings at entry and exit arms with refuge islands.
o Grade-separated crossings (FOBs/subways) may be considered at high
pedestrian volume rotaries.
o Introduce tactile paving, ramps, and adequate lighting for universal accessibility.
• Traffic Calming & Safety Enhancements:
o Use speed calming measures at rotary approaches (rumble strips, markings).
o Improve visibility with advance warning signage, retro-reflective markings, and
street lighting.
o Provide guard rails/barriers at pedestrian crossing points to channel safe
movement.
• Public Transport Integration:
o Relocate bus stops and IPT stands away from rotary mouths to avoid congestion.
o Design designated lay-bys for public transport near, but not obstructing, rotary
circulation.
• Enforcement & Management:
o Deploy traffic wardens at peak hours until signalization is fully operational.
o Introduce CCTV monitoring linked to the Integrated Command & Control Centre
(ICCC).
o Ensure regular maintenance of signals, signage, and markings.
• Split Cycle Offset Optimization Technique (SCOOT)
SCOOT is a tool for managing and controlling traffic signals in urban areas. It is an
adaptive system that responds automatically to fluctuations in traffic flow through the
use of on-street detectors embedded in the road. This system typically reduces traffic
delay by an average of 20% in urban areas. Apart from this, SCOOT also contains other
traffic management facilities such as:
o Bus priority
o Traffic gating
o Incident detection
o On-line saturation occupancy measurement
o Vehicle emissions estimates
SCOOT based traffic management is recommended for all mobility corridors in the city.

With the increase in number of vehicles on roads, city is also experiencing increase in

4.10.1. Regulatory Measures
Limited road capacity, increasing vehicle ownership and limited penetration of public
transport are the main reasons for the present chaotic traffic scenario in the city. The
following regulatory measures are required to bring in improvements in the present
scenario.
a. Transport Demand Management
Transportation Demand Management or TDM refers to various strategies that change
travel behavior (how, when and where people travel) in order to increase transport
system efficiency and achieve specific objectives such as reduced traffic congestion,
increased safety, improved mobility for non-drivers, energy conservation and pollution
emission reductions. TABLE 4.26 gives the TDM Measures used worldwide to manage
the transport demand in the cities.

i. Park and Ride and PT Promotion
Park & Ride facilities and promotion of public transport are the key components of the
strategy adopted to meet the demand in horizon years. Public transport promotion
needs to be carried out through policy interventions as well as awareness programs.
The mass transport system plan detailed in previous sections will promote public
transport and would help to increase its targeted modal share.
ii. Preferential HOV Parking and Carpool Promotion and Coordination
Preferential HOV parking and carpool promotion and coordination provide
opportunities for socializing and reduce commute times through the usage of dedicated
carpool lanes. The designation of premium parking spaces for High Occupancy Vehicles
(HOV) modes is an inexpensive way to encourage employees to carpool or vanpool. It is
intended to make HOV spaces highly valued among employees over single occupant
vehicle spaces. The priority spaces are located close to the building entrances to reduce
the walk time for carpool and vanpool users. Reduced walk times yield a relative
reduction of travel times for HOV users. In addition to demonstrating employer support
for HOV commuting, preferential HOV parking may also reduce the demand for
employee parking spaces. Parking permit fees may also be waived or reduced for HOVs
as an added incentive.
Carpool promotion and coordination is successful when implemented by employers
because they can efficiently market the programs at the workplace and provide
matching functions based on employer records. As employees commute from areas

further away from employment centers to buy affordable housing, vanpools become
increasingly attractive as a means to reduce single-occupant trips.
iii. Alternative Measures
Alternative work-hour programs offered by individual employers such as the
compressed work week, flexi time, and telecommuting are TDM strategies that directly
reduce the number of trips taken by employees to travel to work.
A compressed work week allows employees to work longer days in exchange for an
additional day off that would normally be worked. For example, employees may work
eight nine-hour days and one eight-hour day, in a 10-day (2-week) pay period, totaling
80 hours and permitting one day off each two weeks. In other cases, employees may
work four ten-hour days each week, with one day off each week. This program not only
reduces the amount of peak hour commute trips, but also is often attractive to
employees, increasing morale and job satisfaction.
Other strategies such as “flexi time” or staggered work hours can be used to reduce
peak hour trips and spread trips throughout non-peak times by allowing employees to
begin and end work at a time that is different from the typical 9 A.M. to 6 P.M. work
schedule. Flexi work time can be particularly attractive to employees with commutes
that are congested during peak times, but do not result in the elimination of daily trips
in the manner achieved by the compressed work week strategy.
All over the world, cities have adopted TDM measures to control congestion and
promote public transport. The lessons learnt from the experience suggest that TDM
should be sold as a part of an overall transport strategy. The public has to see the big
picture. TDM is only one part of a package of measures, which included others like
building roads, sophisticated traffic management, priority for bus movements, and new
rail system. All the parts of the package need to be done in parallel to get the desired
result.
b. Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Policy – Rajasthan (2025)
The Government of Rajasthan has notified the Transit Oriented Development (TOD)
Policy, 2025 to promote compact, mixed-use, and transit-supportive urban
development along major public transport corridors. The policy seeks to integrate land-
use and transport planning to increase public transport ridership, reduce reliance on
private vehicles, optimise infrastructure investments, and enable sustainable and
efficient urban growth.
Under the policy, TOD influence zones are delineated within walkable catchments of
mass transit facilities such as metro stations, railway stations and other high-capacity
public transport systems. These zones are envisaged as high-density, pedestrian-
February 2026 Page 4-82
Comprehensive Mobility Plan for Jaipur City
Draft CMP Chapter 4: Development of Comprehensive Mobility Plan
oriented areas supporting a balanced mix of residential, commercial, institutional, and
recreational uses, thereby enabling shorter trip lengths and enhanced access to daily
activities through public transport.
A key aspect of the policy is the provision of development incentives, including
enhanced FAR/FSI and flexible land-use provisions, subject to compliance with
prescribed urban design, access, and infrastructure norms. The policy encourages
reduced parking standards within TOD zones to discourage private vehicle use and
promote modal shift towards public transport, walking, and cycling. Strong emphasis is
placed on Non-Motorised Transport (NMT) infrastructure, including wide and
continuous footpaths, universal accessibility, active street frontage, and safe last-mile
connectivity to transit stations.
The TOD Policy mandates integration with statutory planning instruments such as
Master Plans, Development Plans, and Comprehensive Mobility Plans (CMPs), ensuring
that transit investments are supported by appropriate land-use planning. Development
authorities are required to identify TOD nodes, prepare area-specific TOD plans, and
enable coordinated implementation through close collaboration among urban local
bodies, transport agencies, and infrastructure providers. Institutionally, the policy
encourages the creation of dedicated TOD cells or nodal agencies to facilitate approvals,
inter-departmental coordination, and monitoring of TOD initiatives. Implementation is
largely market-driven, allowing voluntary participation by landowners and developers
while adhering to prescribed planning and design standards.
The policy provides a clear implementation framework through TOD Schemes, classified
as Category-1 (up to 1 ha) and Category-2 (1 ha and above) based on scheme area.
Category-1 schemes must be entirely located within the Intense Development Area
(IDA) of a TOD node, where mixed use is permitted but not mandatory. Category-2
schemes may partially or fully fall within the IDA; however, mixed use is mandatory
across the entire scheme, with at least 25% of the area within the IDA and full inclusion
within the TOD Planning Area. All TOD schemes are required to have access from an
existing road with a minimum Right of Way (ROW) of 18 m, and provisions are made for
plot amalgamation and reconstitution to facilitate integrated and comprehensive
development.
The policy prescribes mixed-use distribution and development intensity through
defined Built-up Area Ratio (BAR) norms based on existing land use and scheme
category. A balanced mix of residential, commercial, and public/semi-public uses is
ensured, while retaining minimum proportions of the original land use. The required
mix may be achieved either horizontally across plots or vertically within buildings,
subject to compatibility and safety considerations. BAR for a TOD scheme is calculated
as the aggregate of BAR entitlements of all constituent plots. For both Category-1 and
Category-2 schemes, the base BAR is as per prevailing Building Bye-laws, with an
enhanced TOD BAR of up to 3.0, subject to a minimum ROW of 12 m. Building height is

payment of a betterment levy, varying by land use and BAR slab, enabling value capture

The National Urban Transport Policy 2014 has recommended setting up of Unified
Metropolitan Transport Authorities (UMTA’s) in million plus cities. The policy document
stipulates following on UMTA
“The current structure of governance for the transport sector is not equipped to deal
with the problems of urban transport. These structures were put in place well before
the problems of urban transport began to surface in India and hence do not provide
for the right coordination mechanisms to deal with urban transport. The central
government will, therefore, recommend the setting up of Unified Metropolitan
Transport Authorities (UMTA’s) in all million cities to facilitate more coordinated
planning and implementation of urban transport programs & projects and integrated
management of urban transport systems. Such Metropolitan Transport Authorities
would need statutory backing in order to be meaningful.”
The metro rail policy - 2017 makes it mandatory for the cities which are planning to have
MRTS to address their mass transport requirements to have city level UMTA. Deloitte
Touche Tohmatsu India Pvt. Ltd. on behalf of MoHUA carried out a detailed study on

4.11.1. Fare Policy for Public Transport
a. Principles for Rational Public Transport Tariff Design
Public transport tariff design is the key for creating an enabling environment for
dynamic and sustainable growth of public transport sector. The fundamental principle
of tariff determination is to ensure that prices lead to an optimum level of investment,
operation, and demand in the sector.
Generally, there is a conflict between the different objectives of fare. For example, to
increase the share of public transport and addressing issues of social sustainability
require that the fares be kept sufficiently low, while efficiency improvement and
viability issues require periodic fare increases with the increase in cost of input of the
service. The agencies in this sector need to balance these objectives to achieve a
sustainable outcome. Similarly, to ensure environmental and social sustainability, it may
be necessary to subsidize public transport operations.
b. Effect on Demand of Bus Services
An increase in public transport fares could lead to modal shift to private modes. Thus,
public transport fares would have to be benchmarked on the cost of alternative modes
of transport to ensure that a modal shift is checked. For addressing issues of social
sustainability, it is imperative that the fares be kept sufficiently low. However, tariffs
should provide incentives for efficiency improvements so as to reduce the cost of
operation.
c. Subsidy Administration
Whenever the government desires that a particular class of consumers be provided
public transport services at subsidized fares, it is recommended that the government to
that effect make the allocation explicitly.
d. Fare Revisions
Fare Revision mechanism should be reasonable, transparent, and accepted to both, the
passenger and the operator. Generally, the fare revision process is not transparent or
scientific. Today the fare revisions are usually a compromise between competing
pressures from operators for an enhancement in the fares and pressures from
commuters for not affecting any increase. Invariably, there is a time lag between such
an increase in the input costs and the increase in fares leading to delays in fleet
augmentation and replacement and thus poor quality of service. However, for

improvements in the service quality fare revisions should be rationalized and made
systematic
e. Integrated Ticketing and Fare Management Systems
To enable seamless, integrated, and user-friendly urban mobility in Jaipur, it is proposed
the implementation of a Unified Mobility Card (UMC) across the city’s public transport
and allied mobility services. The UMC shall serve as a single, interoperable, and cashless
payment instrument for passengers, reducing dependency on multiple tickets and
payment systems.
The proposed UMC shall be aligned with the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC –
One Nation, One Card) framework and shall be implemented through coordinated
efforts of Jaipur Metro Rail Corporation (JMRC) and Jaipur City Transport Services
Limited (JCTSL). The card shall enable seamless travel across Jaipur Metro services
operated by JMRC and city bus services operated by JCTSL, with future integration of
suburban rail services, parking facilities, and other mobility-related services.
Implementation of the UMC is expected to significantly reduce transaction time at
ticketing counters, minimize queuing during peak hours, and improve passenger
convenience and accessibility. The system will support online recharge facilities, mobile-
based integration, and multiple fare products, including passes and time-based tickets,
thereby improving operational efficiency and ridership experience.
The UMC will also facilitate data-driven transport planning and operations, providing
valuable insights into passenger travel patterns, peak demand periods, and modal
interchange behavior. Such data shall support service optimization, rush management
strategies, fare integration and revisions, and capacity planning for public transport.
Phased implementation approach is recommended, with initial deployment across
Jaipur Metro and city bus services, followed by expansion to parking management, park-
and-ride facilities, and other urban transport services

The land in urban areas is limited and there is a limit to the parking space that can be
created in the city. The parking demand is growing with growth of vehicles in Jaipur. The
institutional, public semipublic and busy/commercial areas are major attractors to the
long-term parking. This results in the vehicle parking spilling to streets (main roads or
side streets). One of the important tools to control parking is Parking Pricing. This may
include following measures:
• Levy incremental parking fee on on-street parking
• Off street parking charges to be less than the on-street parking charges

a. Parking Pricing for Core Area
It is proposed to levy incremental parking charges upon on-street parking in the areas

b. Parking Pricing for Area beyond Core Area
Parking pricing for areas beyond core area is proposed to be lower than that of areas
inside the core area. Higher parking charges for internal areas will reduce parking
demand in these congested areas. Similar to parking pricing strategy for internal areas,
short-term parking is promoted for areas beyond core area as compared to long-term
parking by incremental pricing for high rate of parking turnovers.

5.4.1. Implementation Mechanism
The possible areas of the urban transport projects for various implementation
agencies are presented in Table 5.4. Low capital intensive with moderate technical
requirements and high social responsibility projects can be taken up by ULBs. High
capital intensive and more technical required projects like High-Capacity Bus System
and structural projects shall be through the co-operation of State and Central
governments on SPV format with loan from multilateral funding agencies. Projects
with overlapping responsibilities but with high return potentials with less risk and
less gestation period shall be through private sector by BOT/Annuity formats. Private
sector participation will be in the areas of high profitability with less/medium risks.
Hence it is necessary to identify the appropriate areas for different types of private
sector participation for implementing urban transport components. Private sector
involvement in urban transport components can be in following forms:
• Projects with social responsibility on sponsorship pattern (eg: improvement and
maintenance of junctions).
• Annuity format of BOT projects which have less return potentials and high capital
intensive (e.g. Development and maintenance of City Roads in Trivandrum City).
• Commercial projects BOT projects (e.g. Coimbatore Bypass in Tamil Nadu, Bridge
connecting Wellington Island and Mattancherry in Kochi in Kerala).
• PPP for urban bus services (e.g. AICTSL for Indore city bus operation for the bus
services proposed for the Study Area)
5.4.2. Funding Models for Projects Implementation
• Metro system
The financing option for Metro implementation depends upon selection of the
dedicated agency created to implement the project. As per Metro Rail Policy, 2017,
the prominent models are:
o Equity Sharing Model – Special Purpose Vehicle fully under Government
Control: Under this arrangement Government of India and State
Government make equal equity contribution and run SPV as a commercial
enterprise. As per the prevalent practice, Central Government contributes
20% of the project cost as their equity contribution. An equal amount can be
contributed by State Government aggregating the total equity to 40%.
Remaining 60% is arranged as soft loan from funding agencies.
o Public Private Partnership – Design, Build, Finance, Operate & Transfer with
Viability Gap Funding (VGF): The fundamental principle underlying Public

o Grant by the Central Government with Private Participation during

• Development of Terminals (Bus/Freight)
The development of bus and freight terminals may be undertaken through suitable
Public–Private Partnership (PPP) frameworks to ensure efficient delivery, optimal
risk sharing, and long-term operational sustainability. Among the commonly adopted
PPP models are:
o Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) model, wherein the public
authority retains responsibility for financing and operations
o Build–Operate–Transfer (BOT) model, which involves private sector
participation in construction and operation for a defined concession period;
o Design–Build–Finance–Operate–Transfer (DBFOT) model.
The DBFOT model is generally preferred for terminal development, as it integrates
design, construction, financing, and operations under a single concessionaire,
promotes innovation and efficiency, and reduces lifecycle costs while ensuring
improved service quality and asset maintenance over the concession period.
• Development of Multilevel Parking and Public Bike Sharing
The development of multilevel parking facilities may be undertaken through
appropriate Public–Private Partnership (PPP) models to address urban parking
demand in an efficient and financially viable manner. Commonly adopted models
include the EPC model, wherein construction is carried out by a private contractor
with public funding and subsequent operation by the authority, and the Build–
Operate–Transfer (BOT) model. The BOT model is generally preferred for multilevel
parking projects, as it enables private sector participation in financing, construction,
and operation, ensures better asset management during the concession period, and
reduces the financial burden on the public authority.
• Development of Public Bike Sharing
Public Bike Sharing (PBS) systems are typically implemented through a hybrid PPP
model, combining public support in the form of Viability Gap Funding (VGF) with
private sector participation in operations and maintenance. Under this model, the
public authority supports initial capital expenditure and system rollout, while the
private operator is responsible for day-to-day operations, maintenance, and service
quality. This approach has been widely adopted, as it ensures financial sustainability,
operational efficiency, and scalability of the bike-sharing system while promoting
non-motorized and sustainable urban mobility

5.4.3. Indirect sources for funding Urban Transport infrastructure
A number of reports by various organizations have drawn attention to the indirect
values created by transportation projects, suggesting that these could be tapped for
potential funding of the projects themselves. Among the indirect benefits identified in
these reports, the two most important are:
Transit Oriented Development and Land Value Capture: Investments in urban
transport lead to higher property values in developed areas (and to higher municipal
rates linked to those properties), to greater orientation of development along transit
directions, to better anchors for land use planning, etc. Not only do private property
owners gain indirectly from higher values of their holdings around new infrastructure,
sometimes their rights to develop their properties are also gifted freely by cities and
transit systems hoping to boost ridership.
According to various studies, the value is estimated at between 5% - 10% for
residential properties, and between 10% - 30% for commercial properties. To generate
funding from the value created in the proximity zones, a ‘Betterment Levy’ or ‘Land
Value Tax’ can be imposed. This tax is aimed at landowners as it focuses on land value
rather than property value. The tax is designed to capture the value created by the
provision of public services surrounding the areas in which the services have been
provisioned.
Revenue estimation investigates and assesses the potential revenue generation that
may be derived from the transit-oriented development planning initiatives along the
high-capacity bus corridor through various value capture techniques. Revenue from
TOD planning initiatives may be generated through various ways like sale of additional
FSI, revenue from stamp duty, property tax, sale of premium towards ancillaries,
development charges etc.
Property development is the key factor in determining success of a High-Capacity Bus
system. Evidence continues to mount that transit can generate tremendous value by
concentrating development and activity around stations, and that this value can be
captured and used to fund station area improvements and community benefits.
Process of property development requires land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship and
management as major inputs.
Development Rights granted by cities to the areas near the transportation project,
either at very low cost to owners or in some cases free. These benefits could instead
be held in escrow by the transport project itself and made available to property
owners on a paid basis, with the money earned through such transactions available to
under-write a portion of the project costs.

Fuel Cess: Another source of income is from private vehicles through taxes levied on
their consumption of fuel. Typically, cities can add taxes or cess applicable within their
jurisdiction, collecting money for use in making improvements to public transport
schemes. Given the rising use of private vehicles, and the large amounts of money that
can be collected by even a small cess on fuel purchases, this could be an important
source of money for cities.
Urban Transport Tax: Urban Transport Tax or Cess may be levied on the purchase of
new cars and two wheelers.
Carbon Credits: Another source of funds that has emerged in recent years is carbon
credits, typically traded between industrialized countries that operate at high levels of
per-capita pollution, and less industrialized economies where the per-capita climate
impacts are much smaller. In the short run, these credits allow richer economies to
phase out their shift from carbon-intensive production, and also allow poorer
countries to source funds for their project needs. Credits are also available for
countries’ willingness to choose less carbon-intensive choices for their own industries,
and some Indian entities (e.g. bus operators in some states) are examining ways of
seeking such credits for the use of biodiesel in their vehicles. However, the overall
trading scenario around such credits is full of uncertainty and is likely to be
determined by global climate talks. Wherever they are available, however, they can be
tapped to augment other sources of funds.
Unified Mobility Card (UMC): The Unified Mobility Card (UMC) presents significant
opportunities for generating non-fare revenue while strengthening integrated urban
mobility in Jaipur. Revenue can be generated through partnerships with banks and
financial institutions for card issuance, co-branding, and revenue sharing on
transaction fees. The UMC ecosystem also enables float income from stored-value
balances, interest earnings, and settlement efficiencies. Additional revenue streams
may be realized through merchant integrations, allowing the card to be used for
parking, retail outlets, last-mile services, and civic amenities, with a share of
transaction commissions accruing to the implementing agencies. Advertising and
branding rights on physical cards, mobile applications, and associated infrastructure
further provide monetization opportunities.
EV Charging and Battery Swapping Stations: Electric vehicle (EV) charging and battery
swapping infrastructure offers multiple direct revenue opportunities through user-
based charges such as pay-per-use tariffs (per kWh or time-based), per-swap fees, and
subscription or leasing models for commercial fleets including e-buses, e-autos, taxis,
and last-mile delivery vehicles. Battery swapping, in particular, enables predictable
and recurring revenue due to high utilization by fleet operators. Public agencies can
further monetize these facilities through PPP or concession models, wherein private
operators invest, operate, and share revenues via license fees, fixed annuities, or

revenue-sharing mechanisms. In addition, ancillary and indirect revenue streams, such
as land monetization at depots, terminals, parking areas, and transit hubs through
leasing space for charging equipment and allied infrastructure, can significantly
enhance financial viability.
Urban Transport Fund (UTF): As recommended in the NUTP, states and cities are
being encouraged to set up UTFs in order to receive dedicated revenues to be used
exclusively for meeting the needs of urban transport. The NUTP mentions some of the
potential revenue sources for such UTFs, which include a supplement to the petrol and
diesel taxes, a betterment levy on landowners, and tax on employers etc.
Four options for geographical coverage of an UTF have been identified: UTF at the
state level for the whole state; UTF for a particular municipal / urban area; UTF at the
state level for urban areas that do not have their own UTF or UTF for UMTA
jurisdiction.
There are multiple advantages of having UTF at municipal / urban area level. One is
that the funds are specifically available for meeting the urban transport needs of a
single city. Another is that the amount of funding is better known at the local level
than at the state level and therefore a UTF at a municipal / urban area will allow for
better planning. Third is that the use of the funds can better be prioritised according
to the local needs. Since it is envisaged that UMTA should be established at municipal
levels, the preferred option is to have UTF with jurisdiction similar to UMTA
jurisdiction.
Different sources of funds have been identified by different states while setting up
UTFs. In most of the UTFs, a major source of funding is from the Government. This has
taken different forms such as budgetary allocations, government grants, grants
through schemes etc. Several other sources of funds have been identified to
supplement funding from government resources.
Some of these sources of funds are common across various UTFs while others are less
common. For example, cess on vehicle registration is used as a common source of
funding in many of the UTFs. Similarly, betterment levy (which is also a suggested
source of fund in the NUTP) is one of the common sources in some of the UTFs. An
example of a less common source of funding is a premium charged on Transfer of
Development Rights (TDR) which is used by Pimpri Chinchwad Municipal Corporation.
In some of the UTFs, there are provisions of receiving funds from international funding
agencies such as World Bank, ADB etc.
